Consult Summary:
- 50-year-old woman with about 5–6 days of dry cough and runny nose, associated fatigue and nocturnal symptoms; exam suggests an acute viral upper respiratory illness. Has type 2 diabetes and hypertension. Plan focuses on supportive care, safety-netting, and lifestyle modifications; antibiotics considered only if symptoms persist or worsen.

Problem List:

Issue 1:
- Acute viral upper respiratory illness with dry cough and rhinorrhea
  - Onset: started about 5–6 days ago
  - Symptoms: dry, persistent cough (waking her at night), runny nose; throat irritated from coughing; fatigue/weakness; chills; diarrhea began with cough but resolved
  - ROS: no ear symptoms; no chest pain; no dyspnea at rest; no fever documented (shivering reported, fever not confirmed)
  - Exam findings: ears without pain or discharge; no other physical findings documented
  - Social/Med: 50-year-old with type 2 diabetes and hypertension; takes Metformin and Lisinopril; former smoker (quit ~6 months ago); Alcohol use: wine, 2–3 glasses on 3 evenings per week; lives with partner; IT professional
  - Differential/Impression: viral illness; no signs of pneumonia or other acute process identified in the visit

Issue 2:
- Chronic conditions: Type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension
  - Timeline/Status: longstanding; currently on Metformin and Lisinopril; reports condition under regular care and control
  - Medications: Metformin; Lisinopril (dose/route/frequency not documented)
  - Allergies: None
  - Social: living with partner; quit smoking 6 months ago; alcohol use described; not highly active job (IT developer)
  - Exam/Planning: stable chronic disease status referenced; no acute diabetic/hypertensive complications identified during visit
  - Differential/Impression: chronic disease management consistent with baseline control

Issue 3:
- Plan for self-care, follow-up, and lifestyle modification
  - Self-care: rest, fluids, regular paracetamol
  - When to reassess: if no improvement in 2–3 days, return for re-evaluation; if feverish or cough not improving, antibiotics may be considered for chest infection
  - Work: may take 1–2 days off if coughing/infectious; consider return to work early next week if improved
  - Safety-net: return sooner if breathing worsens or symptoms persist/worsen
  - Lifestyle modification: guidance to reduce alcohol intake; suggested reducing to two glasses per week initially, then reassess
  - Chronic disease monitoring: continue existing diabetes and hypertension meds; maintain regular follow-ups with primary care

Medications:
- Metformin (dose/route/frequency not documented)
- Lisinopril (dose/route/frequency not documented)

Allergies:
- None

- Type 2 diabetes mellitus
- Hypertension

Social History:
- Lives with partner
- Former smoker; quit ~6 months ago
- Alcohol: wine, 2–3 glasses on 3 evenings per week
- Occupation: IT developer; not highly active

Preventative History:
- Not documented

Physical Examination:
- Vital signs: not documented
- Ears: no pain or discharge
- Throat: irritated (from coughing)
- Chest/Lungs: not detailed; patient reported no resting breathlessness
- General: fatigued/weak; chills noted

Plan:
- Self-care for viral illness: rest, fluids, regular paracetamol
- Follow-up: return in 2–3 days if not better; if feverish or persistent cough, antibiotics may be considered; return sooner if breathing worsens
- Work: may take 1–2 days off; return to work early next week if improved
- Lifestyle: reduce alcohol intake as discussed (target two glasses/week initially); gradual reduction
- Chronic disease management: continue Metformin and Lisinopril; routine monitoring with primary care
